title: Estimating the pressure-limited CO2 injection and storage capacity of the United States saline formations Effect of the presence of hydrocarbon reservoirs
checked_sections: Selected full-text passages; physical PDF pages 3,6,9
digest: Pressure-limited US saline-formation assessment assigns equally spaced injection wells and uses3D TOUGH2-ECO2N simulations with geological properties and an80%-of-fracture-pressure constraint. Injection fronts/interference, hydrocarbon-reservoir coverage and economic minimum-rate screens govern aggregate development scenarios. The reported Group3-and-higher rates change from1596.8 to682.7 to273.7Mt/y across hydrocarbon-reservoir handling scenarios. The250kt/y/well cutoff is an economic-development filter, not a physical minimum. Pressure-limited capacity is distinct from pore-volume resource and depends on well-development assumptions.
transferability_limits: National aggregate rates and25km spacing do not establish site service, local fracture limits, existing wells or commercial access. Published simulation outputs are useful independent pressure-constrained benchmarks, but a complete annual kr,t array and underlying realisations are not supplied. Constant50-year development scenarios are not observed operations.
original_filename: Estimating the pressure-limited CO2 injection and storage capacity of the United States saline formations Effect of the presence of hydrocarbon reservoirs.pdf

title: Assessment of CO2 geological storage capacity of saline aquifers under the North Sea
digest: 441 candidate sites are assessed with pressure-limited well models; Table 5 reports about 440 Gt capacity and country-level rates.
transferability_limits: Table 5 total rate 22620 Mt/year does not equal country-row sum 14664; scope also includes oil/gas fields. HOLD aggregate annual total pending clarification.

title: Carbon dioxide capture, transport and storage supply chains Optimal economic and environmental performance of infrastructure rollout
digest: Swiss yearly 25-year optimisation models emissions relative to business-as-usual, overseas storage and a delayed hypothetical domestic sink.
transferability_limits: Already covers yearly baseline emissions and domestic/foreign rollout. Fixed transport coefficients and simplified storage differ from detailed coupled operational deliverability tests.
original_filename: Carbon dioxide capture, transport and storage supply chains Optimal economic and environmental performance of infrastructure rollout.pdf

title: Risk management optimization framework for the optimal deployment of carbon capture and storage system under uncertainty
checked_sections: Selected full-text passages; physical PDF pages 3,7,11
digest: Two-stage stochastic CCS deployment framework compares expected cost with variability, probabilistic financial risk and downside-risk metrics. Discrete capture/network decisions couple scenarios, while epsilon constraints trace economic-versus-risk tradeoffs for uncertain carbon-tax conditions. Risk-metric selection changes the types of costly scenarios penalised and the resulting design. Threshold-dependent probabilistic/downside criteria reflect decision-maker preferences; computational difficulty differs with binary risk indicators. The study motivates explicit risk definitions rather than an undefined generic uncertainty score.
transferability_limits: Financial scenario probabilities/subjective thresholds are not empirical failure probabilities, uncertain physical injectivity distributions or a probability of climate benefit. This is prior art for risk-aware planning, not site calibration or a complete lifecycle comparison. No distribution is imported into Paper1.
original_filename: Risk management optimization framework for the optimal deployment of carbon capture and storage system under uncertainty.pdf

title: A scalable infrastructure model for carbon capture and storage_SimCCS
checked_sections: Selected full-text passages; physical PDF pages 3,6,8
digest: SimCCS combines least-cost geographic candidate-network generation with a MILP for source/reservoir opening, discrete pipeline sizes and flow conservation. Source/sink bounds and a system-wide capture target are linked in one atemporal infrastructure decision. The California demonstration uses37 major sources and14 oil-field reservoirs. Aggregation creates cost economies, but the paper explicitly states pipeline construction costs were artificially reduced to emphasise network capabilities. It also states the2009 model is atemporal and each target is reoptimised from scratch.
transferability_limits: Low transport cost is not a transferable realistic price or GHG factor. Approximate radial-injectivity/property formulas have stated domains and do not resolve time-dependent pressure fronts. Original site data/code are needed for exact case reproduction; later dynamic SimCCS versions are not the same original model.
original_filename: A scalable infrastructure model for carbon capture and storage_SimCCS.pdf

title: Optimal design of European supply chains for carbon capture and storage from industrial emission sources including pipe and ship transport
checked_sections: Selected full-text passages; physical PDF pages 4,9,13
digest: Europe-wide economic MILP designs capture at steel/cement/refinery sources, pipeline/ship routes and onshore/offshore storage. Country-specific versus collective European capture targets and storage restrictions are compared; sector-specific capture and multimodal costs enter the supply-chain objective. Offshore-only scenarios require more expensive transport and injection despite similar capture cost. Country-level and Europe-wide targets can change which sources capture CO2, not merely their destination. The paper highlights transnational cooperation requirements alongside economic savings.
transferability_limits: Cost-optimal source selection changes composition, so it is not a matched-source climate comparison. Representing all CCS stages economically does not provide complete lifecycle GHG. Ship-unit-cost sensitivity and projected fleets do not validate operational schedules, pressure-constrained annual service or actual cross-border access.
original_filename: Optimal design of European supply chains for carbon capture and storage from industrial emission sources including pipe and ship transport.pdf

title: Progress and perspectives in source-sink matching for CCUS_A critical review

title: Determination of optimal volume of temporary storage tanks in a ship-based CCS chain
digest: Temporary tank size trades capital cost against production losses. The studied optimum equals the 11,801 m3 ship; different ship sizes can deliver the same availability at different lifecycle costs. No universal buffer ratio follows.
transferability_limits: Korean weather/equipment failure assumptions; excludes unexpected well/reservoir failure.

digest: Dynamic terminal model covers loading, holding, unloading and emergency shutdown. BOG depends on geometry, insulation, ambient temperature, pressure and fill. Two 5,000 m3 tanks serve a 5 Mt/y design; four ships are used in its operational example.

title: Environmental techno-economic assessment of CO₂ maritime transport and offshore sequestration
digest: Compares offshore/onboard injection and onboard capture. The low reported case burden is 8.71 kgCO2/t, but source throughput differs across configurations; it is not adopted as a matched-source whole-chain factor.
transferability_limits: Gate-to-gate; onboard capture changes throughput/denominator. Financial sensitivity direction needs clarification.

title: Flexible Superstructure Synthesis Approach for Multi-Region and Multi-Period CCS Network Design
digest: Multi-region, multi-period synthesis includes time availability, varying CO2 supply and stream quality; a hub supplies temporary storage and mixing. A reported 3% reduction in loss of profit is an economic result, not a climate result.
transferability_limits: Illustrative economic superstructure, not a measured international storage chain.

title: Multi-period superstructure optimization for CCS source-sink matching in South Sumatra industrial clusters
checked_sections: pp1,7–10,12,16; supplement B4-06-S1 Tables S1–S3 and Figures S1–S10
digest: Reservoir-constrained source–sink optimisation links well simulations, readiness and multi-well development. SW-A stores 153.21 Mt and MW-A/MW-D store 159.81 Mt. This supplies a coherent published retention benchmark, but no complete GHG inventory for additional wells/pressure management. Supplement now supplies 14 source rates/costs, 8 capacities/start years/costs, 46 hub distances, and 250 rounded annual injection annotations across three scenarios. Source rates sum to 5.327 Mt/y and 159.81 Mt over 30 years.
transferability_limits: South Sumatra simulation proxy. Supplementary inputs and annual MILP allocation heatmaps are supplied; annotations have one decimal precision. Exact raw allocation output and annual physical maximum injection limits kr,t are not supplied as tabulated data. Capture/well GHG inventory and full network/process inputs remain incomplete.

digest: Seventy-five shipping cases cover 40/80/120 thousand m3 ships, 1–20 Mt/y and 1,000–20,000 km. Fleet counts are integer and BOG reliquefaction/terminal costs are explicit. Published fleet table is retained as model output; the inconsistent density is on hold. The explicit Table1 density now reproduces all75 Table7 fleet counts in a separate operational model; prose units remain unresolved.
